title: BofA stays bullish on a cloud titan that is down 25%
detail:
BofA stays bullish on a cloud titan that is down 25%
Opeyemi Babalola
Mon, September 7, 2026 at 9:33 AM PDT 5 min read
BAC
ORCL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Wall Street's two biggest markets are telling opposite stories about the same company right now. Equity investors keep buying every dip. Credit investors keep demanding more insurance against a default that stock buyers barely seem to consider.

Oracle Corporation (ORCL) sits at the center of that disagreement. Shares have fallen 25% since the company's last earnings report, yet BofA Securities is reiterating a Buy rating and a $240 price target ahead of Thursday's fiscal first-quarter results, according to the BofA note shared with TheStreet.

That target implies nearly 65% upside from current levels. BofA bases its $240 target on a 26.5x calendar-year 2027 earnings multiple, a notable premium over the broader software group's 19x average, arguing that rapid backlog conversion justifies the higher price tag.

This is not the first time Oracle's spending has spooked investors. Shares fell 11% in a single session in December 2025 after a smaller capex increase surprised the market, according to Fortune.

The pattern repeated in June 2026, when a bigger than expected capex figure triggered Oracle's steepest one day drop in six months, according to Bloomberg.

Related: BofA names 2 SpaceX alternatives with massive upside

The math behind BofA's confidence

BofA models cloud infrastructure revenue growing 116% year over year this quarter. That would push Oracle's total revenue growth to 28%, up from 21% in the prior quarter, as parts of Oracle's massive contract backlog begin converting into actual sales.

The acceleration matters because it would be the first hard evidence that Oracle's $638 billion backlog, the largest in enterprise software, is turning from promises into cash.

CNBC reported last week that Wall Street holds 42 buy ratings on the stock against just one sell heading into the print, with consensus estimates pointing to similarly steep growth.

Oracle's slower growing software business is quietly holding up too. BofA expects cloud applications revenue to grow 12.8% this quarter, accelerating from 10.3% in the prior period, while the database business keeps expanding into health care and other industry niches, according to the note.

That legacy engine gives Oracle a profitability cushion the AI infrastructure bet does not have on its own.

That growth is not free. BofA expects gross margin to slip to 63.8% and operating margin to 40%, down from 68.7% and 41.8% a year earlier, as the infrastructure business becomes a bigger share of revenue.

Faster growth and thinner margins are arriving together, which is exactly the tension investors are trying to price.

title: Is Workday a Buy as AI Growth Rises but Valuation Sends Mixed Signals?
detail:
Is Workday a Buy as AI Growth Rises but Valuation Sends Mixed Signals?
Arijit Sarkar

ORCL-PD
SAP
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Workday, Inc. WDAY is pairing double-digit subscription growth with faster AI adoption and improving profitability. Those trends strengthen the long-term business case as recurring demand remains durable.

The investment decision is less straightforward. WDAY's valuation sits slightly above its sub-industry even after compressing well below its own historical median, while competition and execution demands remain material.

Workday's Growth Engine Still Has Visibility

Workday expects fiscal 2027 subscription revenues of $9.94-$9.95 billion, representing 13% growth. That outlook is supported by recurring demand and a customer base that continues to renew at a high rate.

Gross revenue retention remained about 97% in the second quarter, while 12-month subscription revenue backlog rose 14.2% to $9.03 billion. Existing-customer expansion generated roughly 60% of subscription revenue growth, adding another source of visibility.

Workday, Inc. Price and Consensus
Workday, Inc. Price and Consensus

Workday, Inc. price-consensus-chart | Workday, Inc. Quote

WDAY's AI Upside Is Building but Monetization Takes Time

Agentic AI annual recurring revenues approached $600 million, rising more than 200% year over year and 20% sequentially. More than half of net new wins included one or more AI solutions, showing that AI is becoming part of Workday's broader sales motion.

The revenue contribution will not arrive all at once. Management is prioritizing adoption of consumption-based AI products and expects AI to become a more meaningful contributor to incremental annual recurring revenues from fiscal 2028 and beyond.

Workday's Valuation Offers a Mixed Signal

WDAY trades at 4.2X forward 12-month sales, modestly above the Zacks sub-industry's 4.1X. On this measure, the shares carry a small relative premium.

The historical comparison points the other way. Workday's five-year median multiple is 6.7X, well above the current level. The valuation therefore sends a mixed signal rather than placing WDAY clearly at either an obvious bargain or an extreme historical premium.

WDAY Faces Competition and Implementation Risk

Competition remains intense across human capital management and financial software. Oracle Corporation ORCL is building agentic capabilities into Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications, extending AI deeper into enterprise workflows.

SAP SE SAP is also expanding suite-wide agentic AI across SAP SuccessFactors, including recruiting, workforce administration, payroll, learning and talent development. Workday has cited greater deal scrutiny and longer sales cycles in some markets, while complex implementations can delay customer time-to-value.

title: WDAY Jumps 49.7% in 3 Months as AI Momentum Builds: Can it Continue?
detail:
WDAY Jumps 49.7% in 3 Months as AI Momentum Builds: Can it Continue?
Arijit Sarkar
Mon, September 7, 2026 at 7:55 AM PDT 3 min read
WDAY
ORCL-PD
SAP
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Workday, Inc. WDAY shares have gained 49.7% in the past three months, sharply outpacing the broader market. The move puts the durability of the advance in focus as investors weigh stronger operating results against the speed of the recent share-price move.

Subscription growth, rising AI monetization and expanding margins provide fundamental support. Valuation, competitive pressure, longer sales cycles and implementation complexity remain important checks on how much of that operating improvement can translate into further upside.

Workday's 49.7% Rally Meets Stronger Q2 Results

In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenues increased 12.8% year over year to $2.65 billion. Non-GAAP earnings rose 24.4% to $2.75 per share. Both topped the Zacks Consensus Estimate, which called for revenues of $2.63 billion and earnings of $2.62 per share.

Subscription services generated $2.47 billion, up 13.9%, and represented about 93% of total revenues. That mix gives Workday a recurring-revenue base alongside the recent share-price advance.

WDAY's AI Adoption Is Turning Into Contract Value

AI products generated more than $100 million of new annual contract value in the quarter and accounted for more than 25% of total new ACV. Agentic AI annual recurring revenues approached $600 million, rising more than 200% year over year and 20% sequentially.

More than 5,500 customers were using at least one organic Workday agent, up more than 35% from the prior quarter. More than half of net new wins included one or more AI solutions, and more than 200 customers had signed up for Flex Credits.

Workday's Backlog and Retention Support Visibility

Twelve-month subscription revenue backlog increased 14.2% to $9.03 billion, while total subscription backlog rose 8% to $27.4 billion. Those contracted commitments add visibility to Workday's recurring subscription model.

Gross revenue retention held near 97%. Expansion among existing customers drove roughly 60% of subscription revenue growth, while the remaining 40% came from customers added after the start of the comparable prior-year period.

WDAY's Margin Gains Add Weight to the Rally

Non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 31.1% from 29%, with non-GAAP operating income rising 21% to $824 million. Workday attributed the improvement to revenue growth outpacing headcount growth and moderated operating expenses.

Management raised fiscal 2027 non-GAAP operating margin guidance to 31% and expects at least two additional percentage points of expansion in fiscal 2028. The targets matter because total costs and expenses still increased 11% in the July quarter.

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock is flashing a stunning pre-earnings signal as options traders brace for an 11.2% move following its fiscal first-quarter report on September 10.

At $157.62, the implied swing is about $17.65, creating a post-earnings range near $140 to $175. Options do not predict direction. They show the volatility priced into the event.

Wall Street expects revenue of $19.13 billion, up nearly 28%, and earnings of $1.74 per share. The test is whether Oracle can convert AI demand into profitable growth without another spending surge.

Oracle's $638 billion backlog equals 9.5 times its $67.4 billion fiscal 2026 revenue. Cloud-infrastructure sales jumped 93% last quarter, showing demand. However, backlog is not revenue. Oracle must deploy servers and data centers enough to fulfill contracts, recognize sales and collect cash.

The financing tension is clear. Oracle generated $32 billion in operating cash flow last year, yet AI data-center investments drove free cash flow to negative $23.7 billion. The company plans to raise $40 billion during fiscal 2027, increasing investor focus on leverage, funding costs and capital returns.

OpenAI provides a catalyst and concentration risk. Its GPT-6 Astra release supported Oracle shares because OpenAI signed a $300 billion cloud-rental agreement with Oracle last year. Evidence that deployment is progressing could validate Oracle's buildout, while delays would amplify doubts.

Analysts remain bullish. Morgan Stanley raised the target from $207 to $210, while Bank of America maintained a Buy rating and $240 target. Consensus is Strong Buy, with a $254.68 target implying 60.4% upside. Oracle remains down 19% this year.

For investors, the report turns on three metrics: cloud growth, backlog conversion and the capex-to-cash-flow trajectory. Strong sales with deteriorating cash flow may disappoint. Better execution and cash generation could unlock a rebound. With an 11.2% swing priced, the market is preparing to deliver a verdict.

Snowflake's consumption pricing is the point. More AI workloads translate directly into more revenue, so the AI wave acts as a tailwind. Over the last year, SNOW has gained 52%, and it is up 54% year to date through September 4.

Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) report earnings on the same day, September 10, but Bank of America sees the two AI software giants moving in opposite directions.

Analyst Tal Liani maintained a Buy rating and $240 target on Oracle, implying 51% upside, while rating Adobe Sell with a $220 target, implying 17% downside. The contrast reflects one question: Which company is converting AI demand into meaningful financial growth?

Wall Street expects Adobe's fiscal third-quarter earnings to reach $6.08 per share, up from $5.31, as revenue increases 11.7% to $6.69 billion. Those numbers are respectable, but BofA doubts AI is changing Adobe's growth trajectory.

Creative freemium monthly users reached 90 million, rising 70%, while AI-first annual recurring revenue exceeded $500 million, more than tripling. However, AI-first ARR remains below 2% of total ARR.

That gap explains why Liani calls Adobe's strategy largely defensive. AI tools may improve retention and engagement without generating substantial new revenue. BofA expects 11% ARR growth, or 9% excluding Semrush, while higher AI usage costs pressure margins.

Oracle's setup is more aggressive. Wall Street projects earnings of $1.74 per share, up 18.4%, and revenue of $19.13 billion, rising 28.1%. BofA expects infrastructure-as-a-service revenue to jump 116% as roughly one gigawatt of data-center capacity comes online.

Oracle also carries a $638 billion backlog. Yet that opportunity is expensive: BofA forecasts $21 billion in quarterly capital spending and $92.5 billion for the fiscal year. Oracle must prove cloud growth can outrun the resulting cash-flow strain.

Broader analyst sentiment supports the split. Adobe carries a Hold consensus with 1.43% downside, while Oracle has a Strong Buy consensus with 60.4% upside.

For investors, Adobe must show AI adoption accelerating monetization, while Oracle must demonstrate capital efficiency. BofA's preference is clear, but each company faces a different earnings test for shareholders on September 10.

title: Nvidia, Tech Giants Flash Stunning Market Signal

Moz Farooque ACCA

Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Nvidia (NVDA) and major cloud companies are no longer reshaping only the chip market. Their AI buildout is changing supply and demand in long-duration bonds.

Global Macro reported that debt issuance from hyperscalers and Nvidia, including special-purpose vehicles, rose to nearly 70% of U.S. Treasury bond issuance in 2026. The measure uses annual net changes converted into 10-year Treasury equivalents, comparing how much interest-rate duration each group adds.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 4 Warning Signs with NVDA.

Is NVDA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

NVDA GF Value chart

The ratio climbed from about 1% in 2023 to 7% in 2024, 30% in 2025 and nearly 70% in 2026. Between 2015 and 2024, it remained in single- or low-double-digit territory, except for a decline to negative 8% in 2019.

Hyperscalers include companies including Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and Alibaba, which are spending on the data centers, chips and power infrastructure required for AI.

The implication: Investors are absorbing almost as much new duration from this corporate group as the Treasury supplies through coupon issuance. More long-dated corporate paper competes for buyers with government bonds and other issuers. Depending on demand, that added supply could pressure yields and credit spreads or require more attractive pricing.

The figure does not mean these companies borrowed 70% as much as the entire U.S. government. It is a duration-adjusted ratio based on annual net changes. Corporate bonds also carry credit, liquidity and spread risks that Treasuries do not.

For stock investors, the surge shows the AI race is increasingly being financed through balance sheets and special-purpose vehicles, rather than simply operating cash flow. That can accelerate capacity construction but increases exposure to interest rates, refinancing conditions and demand for long-dated debt.

Investors should now watch whether the ratio keeps rising. If AI spending outpaces internal cash generation, corporate duration supply could become a lasting bond-market force. If issuance slows, the extraordinary 2026 spike may prove temporary.

Shares in Oracle have tumbled 18.5% this year and, in July, ratings agency S&P Global downgraded the company's credit rating to one notch above junk status. Oracle has been dogged by broader concerns about the software sector, as well as the debt pile it's amassing in pursuit of becoming a major AI cloud hyperscaler alongside Microsoft, Amazon and Google.

So, naturally, in advance of the company's upcoming earnings report on Thursday, some analysts see a golden buying opportunity.

The Big Fundamentals

Investor concerns about Oracle center on spending and debt. The evidence to justify them is easier to spot than a California transplant in Austin, where the company is headquartered.

Oracle's June earnings release revealed negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion in the 2026 fiscal year. Revenue was devoured by capital expenditures, mostly in connection with AI buildout plans that include future data center leases totaling $260 billion. Financing those plans to build enormous amounts of new cloud infrastructure pushed Oracle's debt pile up to $129.5 billion. 

But Jefferies analysts argued last week that Oracle's fundamentals deserve a second look. Quarterly revenue growth finished the 2026 fiscal year at 21% after starting the year at 12%. Oracle's contracted backlog rose a whopping 363% in the 2026 fiscal year to a record $638 billion. Revenue climbed 17% to $67 billion. With "most bad news priced in," the stock may be on the cusp of a buying opportunity:

While they cut their price target to $290 from $320, that still suggests an 82% upside from Friday's $158.78 closing price.

Morgan Stanley analysts said Oracle could report annualized cloud revenue growth of up to 63% in its most recent quarter, driven by its GPU-as-a-service business, in what would act as a "good setup" for the stock.

Good News From Rivals: Cloud providers Nebius Group and CoreWeave recently offered optimistic commentary on AI pricing, which Morgan Stanley said bodes well for Oracle's earnings. A recent run of rallies by rival software firms is another good sign, as investors have shown renewed interest in the beaten-down sector. Salesforce, Okta and Snowflake all jumped 17% or more after reporting across-the-board earnings beats in the past two weeks.
